name: Walmart

profile.address: Federal Drive, Colorado Springs, El Paso County, Colorado, 80921
profile.reading:
On Federal Drive in the Colorado Springs area of El Paso County, Colorado, Walmart operates an enterprise data center that the company built and brought into service with unusually little public fanfare. Site work and construction in the area were reported locally years before Walmart's involvement was confirmed, and permitting and construction filings did not initially identify the retailer as the entity behind the project, which for a time fueled speculation in the Colorado Springs business community about who was building a large, unmarked technical facility on the city's north side. The Colorado Springs Gazette and the trade publication Data Center Dynamics both eventually reported that Walmart was the owner, with Data Center Dynamics noting the company brought the site online quietly rather than through a formal announcement or ribbon cutting, a pattern consistent with how Walmart has handled several of its other internal data center projects around the country.

Public reporting has put the construction investment at roughly 100 million dollars, though no source has published the facility's critical IT capacity in megawatts, its total square footage, or a tenant list, because it is not a leased or colocation building. Walmart operates the site for its own internal use, folding it into the backbone of technology infrastructure that keeps the company's e-commerce platform, supply chain and inventory systems, and in-store point of sale and logistics technology running across its stores and distribution network. As the largest retailer in the world by revenue, Walmart has built out a substantial private data center footprint over the past decade to support that scale of operation, and the El Paso County site fits that broader pattern of enterprise capacity rather than public cloud or wholesale colocation space.

Colorado Springs, with its relatively low natural disaster risk, access to Colorado's power grid, and proximity to the Front Range's fiber routes, has attracted a mix of enterprise and government computing facilities over the years, and Walmart's decision to locate here follows that same logic even though the company has said little publicly about why it chose the site. Because the facility serves Walmart's own operations rather than outside customers, the company has no commercial incentive to publish capacity, uptime, or sustainability figures the way a colocation provider courting tenants would, and as of this writing none of that detail is publicly available.

reading:
Walmart is the largest retailer in the world by revenue and a New York Stock Exchange listed company that files annual reports with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission. It sits in this registry as an enterprise operator, meaning it builds and runs computing capacity for itself and sells none of it. The registry holds one United States row for the company, an enterprise data centre on the north side of Colorado Springs in El Paso County, Colorado.

The clearest public record of that building is an economic development record rather than a technical one, which is typical for enterprise projects that never market space. Local officials approved a tax incentive package worth 4.5 million dollars in May 2011, at a point when the company behind the project had not been publicly identified. Walmart bought a 24 acre parcel in September 2011, and the 210,000 square foot building came online in October 2012 at a reported construction cost of about 100 million dollars. Officials projected roughly 488 million dollars of economic impact over fifteen years. Neither the company nor the city marked the opening with an announcement or a ribbon cutting, which is why local coverage of an unidentified developer building a large unmarked technical facility ran ahead of any confirmation, and why the region treated the project as a significant win without ever holding a public event for it. That sequence, an incentive vote before the applicant is named, is common enough in data centre siting that it is worth recognising as a pattern rather than as secrecy peculiar to one company.

The power record is empty. No IT load, no utility service size, no standby generator rating and no on site generation figure has been published for this building by the company, by the city, by the county or in any filing. The construction cost and the 210,000 square foot building area are the only physical numbers on the record, and the square footage is gross building area rather than white space. Dividing cost by area, or applying a watts per square foot assumption to a gross figure, produces a capacity number that no source ever stated, and this registry does not carry one for that reason.

The site's geography is worth reading correctly. The stored street value on this row is a reverse geocode to Federal Drive, a nearest road answer rather than a verified postal address. The stored coordinates place the building roughly a fifth of a mile from the separately recorded SAP site, which sits on T5 Data Centers' 64 acre restricted use campus nearby. The two are entirely distinct projects on distinct parcels, Walmart's 24 acres bought in 2011 and SAP America's purchase of roughly 9 acres from T5 in 2016, and their proximity reflects the clustering of large computing buildings along the Federal Drive and InterQuest corridor. That corridor draws them for the same reasons in each case, comparatively cheap utility power, dry high altitude air that permits free cooling for most of the year, and low exposure to natural hazards. Finally, a facility count of one describes what this registry holds in the United States for Walmart and is not a statement about the company's total computing footprint, which Walmart does not enumerate publicly.
